analysis.one_liner: Raises SNAP food benefits by basing them on the low-cost food plan instead of the cheaper thrifty plan.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 117 Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee vote, a hearing, or a floor vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise monthly food assistance (SNAP) benefits for low-income households by switching the government's benefit formula from the cheapest official food budget, the thrifty food plan, to the somewhat more generous low-cost food plan. It would also raise the minimum benefit to $50, create a standard deduction for out-of-pocket medical costs for elderly or disabled members, remove the cap on the housing-cost deduction, and exempt childless adults from work requirements if no job slot in a SNAP employment and training program was offered to them.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households receiving SNAP, especially those hit by the benefit formula: households with high housing costs that currently hit the shelter-deduction cap, households with elderly or disabled members facing medical bills, and childless adults unable to find a spot in an employment and training program who would otherwise lose benefits after three months. Residents of Puerto Rico and American Samoa would see their nutrition block grants tied to the higher food plan.
analysis.who_benefits_short: SNAP households and low-income food buyers

how_it_helps.text: Bases benefit amounts on the USDA low-cost food plan rather than the thrifty food plan, which produces a higher monthly allotment for nearly all SNAP households [S2][S3].
Raises the minimum monthly benefit for the smallest, lowest-income households to $50 for fiscal year 2017 levels [S3].
Creates a $140 standard medical expense deduction for households with an elderly or disabled member, adjusted for inflation in later years [S3].
Eliminates the cap on the deduction for excess shelter expenses, so households paying high rent or utilities no longer have that cost ignored in the benefit calculation [S2][S3].

Exempts able-bodied adults without dependents from work requirements if they are not offered a position in a SNAP employment and training program, so they do not lose benefits for failing to meet a requirement no program slot existed to fill [S2][S3].
Raises and inflation-adjusts the nutrition assistance block grants for Puerto Rico and American Samoa based on the low-cost food plan [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through higher spending on SNAP. The shift to the low-cost food plan raises the benefit basis for nearly all participating households, so the annual cost of the program rises substantially; state agencies would also rework eligibility calculations to apply the new deductions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, via higher USDA spending

drawbacks.text: The bill substantially raises federal SNAP spending by moving nearly every household to a higher benefit basis, a cost an honest supporter has to weigh against its targeted increases for the smallest households and high-rent families [S3].

Critics of the work-requirement exemption argue that exempting childless adults whenever no employment and training slot is offered reduces the pressure to work and could shrink program slots further; the bill does not fund new positions beyond the existing program structure [S3].
The benefit formula still bases allotments on a family-of-four diet adjusted for household size, so some household compositions may still be poorly matched to actual food costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in eight Americans who receive SNAP, the bill's benefit increases are meaningful and targeted at the people the current formula shortchanges: high-rent households, households with medical costs, and the smallest households. The cost is real but is the ordinary cost of a larger anti-hunger program, and the bill's structure — automatic annual updates tied to food costs — makes the increases durable rather than one-time. The weakest element is the work-requirement exemption, which fixes a real unfairness (people punished for a lack of program slots) but does not expand the programs that would give those people actual work experience.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its Nutrition subcommittee, where it sat without a markup, hearing, or vote until the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Alma Adams introduced the bill on March 1, 2017 with 30 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Agriculture the same day, and on March 23, 2017 to the subcommittee on Nutrition [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee markup, a hearing, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].
It accumulated 117 cosponsors over its lifetime, every one of them a Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new benefit. SNAP households kept the lower benefit levels calculated on the thrifty food plan, and the federal budget avoided the added cost of the expansion. The bill's cosponsors and the low-income households it aimed to help were left with nothing enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: SNAP households, who got no increase

for.name: Rep. Alma Adams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 30 original cosponsors; the bill carries her name as sponsor.

for.name: 117 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the second-largest cosponsor list any single bill typically attracts, but no Republican joined.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture (Chair Mike Conaway)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, assigned it to the Nutrition subcommittee, and never scheduled it for a markup, hearing, or vote; the bill saw no committee action after March 23, 2017.

sides.party_line_note: All 117 cosponsors were House Democrats; not a single Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-chaired Agriculture Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: SNAP benefits are spent at grocery stores, so higher benefit amounts would have translated into more food purchases at these retailers. Their interest in larger SNAP allotments runs alongside recipients' interests.
Moving the benefit basis from the thrifty to the low-cost food plan raises federal SNAP spending for nearly all participating households, so the cost of the program would have grown substantially.
